# Study finds AI chatbots frequently miss possible diagnoses

## The research from Mass General Brigham raises concerns about medical advice people are getting from artificial intelligence.

#### By Brianna Borghi • Published May 21, 2026 • Updated on May 21, 2026 at 10:58 pm

Experts are saying technology can miss critical information in diagnosing medical conditions.

As more people turn to artificial intelligence for medical advice, experts are warning the technology may not always provide reliable answers.

A new study from Mass General Brigham found popular AI chatbots frequently missed possible diagnoses when evaluating patient symptoms, raising concerns about how patients use the tools to make health care decisions.

"When I have a worry about something, I definitely use it, and to ask questions," said Abby Patz, a college student.

Others say they have used chatbots to help decide whether symptoms were serious enough to seek medical care.

"I've been in a situation where I was experiencing symptoms, like whether or not I should go to urgent care versus going to the ER," said Korina Schulman, a dental hygienist.

A recent Gallup poll found one in four Americans have used AI for health information or advice.

But Dr. Marc Succi, executive director of the MESH Incubator at Mass General Brigham and an associate professor at Harvard Medical School, said the technology still falls short of a trained physician.

"I don't think there's any chatbot publicly available, or medically specific, that is remotely as good as a physician," Succi said.

Succi and his research team tested 21 large language models, or LLMs, to see how they evaluated patient symptoms. The study found the chatbots failed to identify all possible diagnoses in 80% of cases.

"If you're a patient and you're using it, the concern is that you don't necessarily have the training to critically appraise the output and know what's missing from those differential diagnoses," Succi said.

Researchers found the chatbots performed significantly better when users provided all relevant medical information. In those cases, the models identified the correct final diagnosis 90% of the time.

"You can get your medical records and upload them. Obviously, there's privacy concerns, so it's a personal risk-benefit tool," Succi said. "I think part of the issue is uploading the right amount of information, and the right information to begin with."

At the same time, a new report from the nonprofit patient safety organization ECRI named AI chatbots the top health technology hazard of 2026.

"These are not FDA-regulated tools," said Dr. Scott Lucas, vice president for devices, therapeutics, and technology at ECRI. "It's not mandatory to report problems associated with the use of the chatbots like a medical device is."

ECRI's report warns chatbots can recommend unsafe treatments, suggest unnecessary testing, and potentially worsen health care disparities if they are trained on biased data.

"Use them as a tool for information, collect all that information, you become a very educated patient, take that to your provider, and you can have a good, informed discussion," Lucas said. "But don't make rash decisions based on the output alone."

Experts say AI chatbots can still be useful tools for patients, but they stress the technology should supplement – not replace – the advice and guidance of medical professionals.
